Hold'Em Poker Manager is a tool to help Poker players to keep track of their games. Running games and past games are supported.

The UI is extremely user friendly, with material design, which makes it easy and extremely fast to record all game details, avoiding to use it extensively on the poker tables. Just start the session with the starting info and put the phone away. When the game is over, just stop it and input the results and it is done.

The app generates charts and reports based on the user inputs, that allows her to see the evolution of her game!

The free version is just a demo, that limits the app to create 10 sessions.

There are so many tips and lists but what works? If there is one tip above all others you'd offer the writing comity what would it be?

Editing is the crux of all writing. You'll write a first draft only a single time, but revise that over and over until you've refined the merit of that original draft into something that readers are willing to engage in. Most (myself included) rarely edit enough.

Doing so makes your writing so much more powerful.

Just do it.

Whether it's the grand lifelong project or a daily prompt, find a way to write, and leave any lingering concerns or anxiety about its merits for the edit.

During your initial draft duct tape your inner critic and throw that bitch in the closet. Your first draft will suck, let it suck, let it be terrible and so horrific that when you go to edit it the first time you cringe, the key being that you have produced something to edit in the first place. Stop comparing your first practice to someone's highlight reel or you'll never get out of the blocks.

Just my opinion.

So, you write on your laptop, do you?

Find the wireless connectivity switch - the physical button - and turn it off.

Good lord does it help for productivity.
Read more than you write. You'll notice a huge different not only in how easily things come to you but in the development of your overall style.

Don't listen to, or ask for, advice. I enjoy reading the novels of people who offer writing advice; they tend to be mediocre at best, and dreadful at worst. Bear in mind that James Patterson and E.L. James now imagine themselves qualified to offer advice on writing. Neither are. It should be obvious to anyone remotely discerning that they are nothing more less than vulgar cash-in chancers. Don't mistake people who know what sells with those who have artistic insight. The latter are much rarer, though these days it's regarded as elitist to say so. We live in a populist age.

Just write. Period.

Also, when writing for an audience, trust them just a little. Think about what needs to be described and what doesn't.

I hope you all enjoy Voat as much as I do, and welcome aboard!
